newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka cigarette maker takes on the smugglers.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka cigarette maker takes on the smugglers.

text.p: B.A.T. Industries Plc's Sri Lankan subsidiary, Ceylon Tobacco Company Ltd (CTC), has declared war on smuggled cigarettes that bite deeply into its earnings, a senior company official said on Tuesday.

CTC, Sri Lanka's monopoly cigarette maker and largest listed corporate in terms of turnover, will start selling its British parent company's Benson & Hedges cigarettes in addition to locally made Bristol and Gold Leaf to help defend its market share against smuggled cigarettes.

"We have priced a pack of 20 Benson & Hedges at 100 rupees ($1.8) against smuggled cigarettes which range between 75 and 90 (about $1.4 to $1.6) rupees for the same quantity," Mick Fenn, CTC's chairman, told Reuters.
CTC strategy was to stress that its products were fresh and legal, he said.
CTC said the dual impact of smuggling and rises in government excise duty was eating into its revenues to the extent that it was unable to see an adequate return on investments.
CTC has invested 300 million rupees a year since late 1993 when it kicked off a plan to restructure the company by reducing debt and improving productivity and efficiency.
The government had raised the excise duty on tobacco sales three times in the past 18 months which had negated the good work on restructuring, Fenn said.
"Though profits in 1995 rose by 67 percent over 1994, in real terms the company has only got back to where it was in 1989," he said.

The company was left with 11 percent of its turnover of 15.8 billion rupees in 1995 as the balance went in excise duty and other forms of tax, he said. CTC accounts for about 10 percent of the government's annual tax revenue.

The company says that 30 to 40 million smuggled cigarettes, comprising about eight percent of total monthly consumption, find their way to the market and it is lobbying the government to impose stiffer penalties on smugglers.
"The present law, under which a meagre fine is imposed and the goods released or auctioned, is toothless," says Fenn.

A senior customs official said: "When a large quantity of smuggled cigarettes is detected we impose a fine at least equal to the value of the goods, confiscate and give the cigarettes to the armed services."
But he said that cigarettes could come in undetected, as it was impossible to check all containers coming to Sri Lanka.
Analysts believe the company would be able to increase revenue significantly by plugging leaks through smuggling.

The company saw turnover of 8.4 billion rupees in the first half of the financial year to June 30 and net profit of 230.9 million, up from 8.0 billion and 194.18 million in the same period the previous year.
